sources.text: President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi had called on Egyptian lawmakers to authorize military assistance to the kingdom, saying any support would be defensive.

sources.headline: Egypt pledges support for Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
sources.text: Sisi has asked for an urgent parliamentary session to authorise the military to help defend Saudi Arabia should the kingdom request its assistance.Egypt on Sunday announced that it was ready to militarily assist Saudi Arabia for safeguarding its security and stability, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis step up their assaults on the world’s largest oil exporter.Sisi has asked for an urgent parliamentary session to authorise the military, one of the largest and most powerful in the region, to help defend Saudi Arabia should the kingdom request its assistance.“Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites,” the Egyptian Presidency said in a statement, according to Reuters.The statement came after a meeting of Egypt’s National Defence Council, which was chaired by President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi. The parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief also attended.In a speech on Saturday, Sisi said Egypt would act in line with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The crown prince had visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen flared up again.In recent days, the Houthis have targeted Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco. The attacks come amid renewed clashes with the Saudi-backed forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, following the collapse of a truce.Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. After the military removal of Islamist President Mohamed Morsi in 2013, Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states supplied Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments.Egypt had earlier joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to back the government against the Houthis, although its combat role was limited.

sources.headline: Egypt says ready to back Saudi Arabia in war against Iran-allied Houthis
sources.text: CAIRO, Oct 18 - Regional military power Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, potentially raising the stakes in the Middle East war as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on the kingdom.Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the Arab world's largest, to help defend its Gulf Arab ally if the kingdom requested its support.A parliamentary vote had been expected on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said.Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the north, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.Any Egyptian military backing for Saudi Arabia could mark a major escalation in the wider Iran war, which has threatened global energy supplies and sent oil prices soaring since the US and Israel attacked the Islamic Republic in late February.Hours after an announcement on further discussions by the parliament, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said in a post on X that he discussed regional developments and the importance of de-escalation during a phone call with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan.HOUTHIS RAMP UP ATTACKS ON SAUDI ARABIAThe Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with Saudi-backed forces. The Houthi advances threaten the strategic Bab el-Mandeb oil shipping route, following the collapse of a truce."Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.The statement followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.If Egypt weighs in, it could face attacks by the Houthis, ragtag mountain fighters who have emerged as a deadly force of tens of thousands and whose missiles and drones threaten the region.Arab countries, especially Gulf states hosting US bases, have faced repeated attacks by Iran and its allies, including the Houthis and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq, during the conflict.Egypt's Mediterranean port of Damietta came under a drone attack in July with no group claiming responsibility. Egypt has not blamed any party for the attack but said it was taking necessary measures to protect the country's national security.Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states including the United Arab Emirates provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist President Mohamed Morsi in 2013. Sisi became president a year later.Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role in the civil war.Riyadh has turned to regional allies and Pakistan after it sought US President Donald Trump's help to fight the Houthis. Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing.Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman visited Abu Dhabi on Sunday and met with UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with talks focusing on regional security, according to the Emirati state news agency.The talks followed a visit to Riyadh last month by UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the first trip by a senior UAE official to the kingdom since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year. REUTERS

sources.headline: Saudi Arabia strikes oil depots in Yemen and says missiles launched toward location of Saudi Aramco HQ
sources.text: Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco.The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces. Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz.Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left 300 injured. The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.A Houthi spokesperson responded to the attack on its oil storage by warning “all employees and citizens present near any facility affiliated with Aramco Petroleum in Riyadh to evacuate it and stay away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces”.Later in the day, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired at Dharan, the location of the headquarters of Saudi Aramco. It said fragments from the interception fell on a residential area. Witnesses reported hearing loud booms. An evacuation order ​for the building ‌had been ‌issued, four sources told Reuters. There was no official comment ​or ​confirmation ​from ​Aramco.The incident underlined how Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while the Houthis have to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology. Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted. They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect. They are cheap and it does not take many to get through to be effective”.But the two sides’ dramatic threats to set ablaze the enemy energy infrastructure symbolised how the conflict is escalating rather than blowing itself out.A map released by the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition shows the targeted site of the Yemeni Oil Company and Al-Sabaha Central station in Sana’a. Photograph: @CJFCS.Donald Trump complained that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and said he would “never forget” their attacks, which he suggested were an attempt to influence the US midterm elections next month. But he stopped short of announcing any new military action.The latest phase of the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transportation of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.This week, the Houthis have come closer to throttling the southern city of Taiz, drawing close enough to the city edges to fire rockets into residential areas. City leaders have made repeated appeals to the Yemeni government for military equipment while public health professionals warned of a shortage of medicines for patients in intensive care.Government-aligned forces sent reinforcements to the south-western district of Al-Mudarabba in Lahij governorate as well as the mountain district of Al-Waz’iyya.But anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen are not themselves united: a group known as the Southern Transitional Council has been taking a more prominent role in the fight against the Houthis – even though its main objective is to secede from the country’s north.On Tuesday, Aidarous al Zubaidi, the exiled STC leader, gave a rare address declaring “a popular mobilisation in defence of the south, and its national liberation project” – including by repelling the invading Houthi militia.Al Zubaidi, now based in Abu Dhabi, made clear he still supported a plan to eventually hold a referendum on the independence of South Yemen.Zubaidi’s organisation remains banned in Yemen and he has been charged with treason, but there are incremental behind-the-scenes talks under way testing whether the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman is prepared to legitimise the STC and even permit Zubaidi to return. Reinstatement of the STC would be seen as a betrayal by the current Yemen president, Rashad al-Alimi, but his usefulness to Saudi Arabia is reduced if he does not have the same military forces at his disposal as Zubaidi.

Houthis threaten escalation after strike on Saudi oil giant Aramco 
 
  Middle East   
 Yemen's Houthi rebels said Wednesday they had targeted facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco after officials in Riyadh reported a strike on a building in an area housing the energy giant's headquarters. The Iran-back militia also claimed missile strikes on the capital Riyadh and vowed to continue attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities.   
 
 
 
 
Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 18:21
    3 min Reading time   
  Share     
 
  By:  
 
  FRANCE 24     
  Video by:  
 
  Eliza HERBERT

 Cover image: Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh following a Houthi attack on October 3, 2026. © AFP  
 
    
 
 
   01:47    
     
 
Yemen's Houthis vowed on Wednesday to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, a day after a strike that sources said caused extensive damage to the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco.  
The Houthis said the threatened locations were legitimate targets and described their attacks as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemen – threatening to escalate a conflict reignited by the US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.  
Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people.  
Read moreSaudi Arabia threatens 'decisive' response after Riyadh airport strike kills at least 12 
Tuesday night's attack on Saudi Aramco's base in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a fire that spread across several floors, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters. The Saudi energy ministry had said the strike caused a limited fire.  
Operations at Aramco were continuing normally, with employees working from home, according to two of the sources. Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment. 
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the Iran-backed group had conducted "a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran", as well as strikes targeting Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital. 
He added the attacks were carried out with missiles and drones, and that operations "will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities". 
Saudi-led forces say they intercept missile 
The escalating conflict has dealt a blow to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's ambitious plans to transform and diversify the Saudi economy and reduce its reliance on oil.  
The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom's backing of Yemeni government forces in the Yemen war that restarted last month.  
The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday, and several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.  
Saudi authorities earlier issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh on Wednesday before the warning was lifted, a witness said. It wasn't immediately clear what caused the booms and there was no immediate comment from the authorities on their source.  
The Saudi government media office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about the cause of the booms.  
Read moreBlasts rock Riyadh as Houthis target Saudi airports, oil facilities 
In their statement on Wednesday, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at the Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, Riyadh airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh.  
In a broad threat, they urged "international shipping companies", civilians and workers to evacuate Saudi airports and oil facilities.

The Dhahran complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.  
Riyadh’s international airport has come under attack four times, including Saturday's attack which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade.  
Authorities have closed the airport until October 17, and airlines have canceled flights to Saudi Arabia.  
Yemen hospitals overwhelmed, Red Cross warns 
Fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in support of the government in 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.  
The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year.  
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Red Cross said on Wednesday that hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as fighting intensified along multiple front lines.  
The UN World Food Programme warned that life-saving assistance had been cut off to the government-held city of Taiz, which was encircled by Houthi fighters earlier this month.  
"WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children," WFP said in a statement.

sources.headline: More explosions heard in Saudi Arabia as pressure mounts on US to respond
sources.text: More explosions have been heard in the Saudi capital, with suspicions once again falling on the Houthi rebels from Yemen.

sources.headline: As the Houthis escalate attacks, Saudi Arabia faces a 'huge problem'
sources.text: Deadly attacks on Saudi Arabian airports in recent days, plunging air travel across the kingdom into chaos, have marked a dangerous new escalation in the country's long-running conflict with Yemen's Houthi rebels.And as the smoke had barely cleared from an attack on Riyadh airport that killed 13 people, the Iranian-backed group issued an ominous warning: the worst is yet to come.It is another concerning development in a region already grappling with a grinding stalemate in another war, as talks between the US and Iran go nowhere fast.The situation also presents a challenge for Saudi Arabia, which has spent years trying to assert its dominance in the region and reinvent its image as a haven for investment and opportunity.Experts say the attacks have highlighted gaps in the Saudis' defences, with some reports suggesting the country is running low on defensive missiles.Resolving the crisis might be impossible without a deal to end the broader war between Washington and Tehran — and even then, it is not entirely clear-cut."The Houthis, in some sense, have been and remain a proxy, a partner of the Iranians, but they're increasingly independent-minded," former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney told the ABC."In a strange way, that's especially dangerous — the idea that the Houthis might no longer be an Iranian proxy means that they can no longer be influenced simply by cutting a deal with Iran."And they're highly ideological, highly belligerent towards the Saudi monarchy and [have] become this huge problem in their own right."Why are the Houthis and Saudi Arabia fighting?In 2015, the Saudis intervened in the civil war in Yemen, backing the country's internationally recognised government against the Houthis.The paramilitary group — designated a terrorist organisation by several countries, including Australia — had been demanding greater autonomy for the areas it controlled, and wanted to oust the Yemeni government.Since the Houthis took control of the capital, Sanaa, as well as northern and western Yemen, Saudi Arabia has been supporting the government in the south.The Houthis, a listed terrorist organisation in Australia, emerged in the 1990s. (Supplied)Part of the Saudis' support included a blockade of Yemen, contributing to the humanitarian crisis inside the country.The conflict raged until a ceasefire was brokered between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis, enforced from March 2022.Fast forward to the middle of this year when the truce was shattered.The Saudis launched air strikes on Yemen's international airport in Sanaa in July, targeting the runway in a bid to stop an Iranian plane from landing. The Houthis, in response, launched missiles at a regional Saudi airport.These were the opening salvos in what has since become a major escalation.The Houthis also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, threatening to effectively block the narrow Bab el Mandeb Strait through which the Saudis dispatch millions and millions of barrels of oil to global markets.The group said the blockade was in response to Saudi Arabia's "oppressive siege" on Yemen over the past 12 years.Airport attacks mark 'difficult' escalationWhile the Houthis have been attacking the Saudis for months now, the situation has changed.In recent days, multiple strikes have hit King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh, including one attack on Saturday as the airport was full of pilgrims travelling to visit Muslim holy sites in Mecca and Medina.The strike killed 13 people and injured more than 300, making it one of the largest mass casualty attacks in recent Saudi history, said Thomas Juneau, a professor from the University of Ottawa's Graduate School of Public and International Affairs."We have seen the Houthis over the years targeting with missiles or drones critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, oil infrastructure, airports, the Formula One race a few years ago," he told ABC Radio National."But what we are seeing … is an escalation."The Houthis escalated its attacks on Saudi Arabia by bombing the Riyadh airport last week. (AP)The situation has tested Saudi air defences, with reporting in media outlets including the Wall Street Journal suggesting the country may now be running low on interceptor missiles."[The Houthis] can fire like tens of drones and missiles and at least one of them … will cause the damage," Maysaa Shuja Al-Deen, senior researcher at the Sana'a Center, told the ABC."They don't aim to destroy the whole facility. It's only to harm it, to cause the damage is enough for them."It's very difficult with this kind of weapons to assure or to guarantee that you have a defence system that guarantees 100 per cent protection."Mr Ratney said the Saudis would be looking for any help they could get from the US, even if predicting how US President Donald Trump might respond to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's requests for assistance was difficult."The Saudis have considerable air defences, including Patriot missile batteries — they have probably more than most countries in the world at this point, but it's obviously not enough," he said."It's a huge country and, when you think about it, they're going to prioritise their energy infrastructure, particularly in the east."And I think in some ways, they didn't totally factor in the potential for the Houthis to start targeting areas like civilian airports."Why Saudi-Houthi negotiations will be 'difficult'Ms Shuja Al-Deen said the Houthis currently have the upper hand in the conflict, complicating any deal to end it."It's very difficult to sit at the negotiation table and assume that everyone will give all the concessions for the Houthis based on this military situation — and now also because the Yemeni war is now overlapping with the regional war," she said.Houthi supporters rallying in Yemen's capital on October 9. (Reuters: Mohammed al-Mahdi)Professor Juneau said the objective behind the Houthis' escalation was to "continue to build their leverage relative to Saudi Arabia"."One day, I have no idea when, and not in the short term, but one day there will be negotiations for some kind of political resolution between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis," he said.Mr Ratney said it was an issue that needed greater international focus, as it went "beyond Saudi Arabia"."And sooner or later, I think the West, the Middle East, are going to have to figure out a way to deal with it," he said."I think from the Saudi and broader Gulf perspective, that's uncertainty that they don't need right now."They just want this war de-escalated, and they want to be able to get back to, in the case of Saudi Arabia, their whole economic transformation initiative, investment, tourism, everything that they've been working towards."

6:31 AM / October 16, 2026
Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to "ecocide"
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday urged countries to condemn what he called "ecocide" in the Middle East caused by "wars of aggression" against his country.Pezeshkian said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had taken a significant toll on nature that extended beyond national borders and required "international solutions.""What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned," Pezeshkian said at a nature summit in Armenia that was attended by United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.Pezeshkian decried an "atmosphere of distrust" between Iran and the U.S. in a recent interview with CBS News. "As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said. "Every day, they increase the sanctions against us. Every day, they threaten us. Every day, they strike us, and they don't honor what they have put in writing. So, if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?"CBS/AFP
8:09 PM / October 15, 2026
Rubio tells Lebanon's president not to return seized explosives to Hezbollah
Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Lebanon's president on Thursday not to return several hundred kilograms of explosives which Lebanese authorities seized last week from the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah, a State Department official told CBS News.In a call, Rubio asked Lebanese President Joseph Aoun "to hold accountable all those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment, and underscored that returning explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question," the official said. The explosives had been seized on a road linking eastern Lebanon to Beirut, a Hezbollah lawmaker acknowledged earlier Thursday.Rubio on the call also brought up "Lebanon's 1955 Boycott Law," the official said, which prohibits any contact between Lebanese and Israeli citizens.Rubio told Aoun the law is "routinely used for politicized prosecutions that deter steps towards peace," the official said. The secretary of state called the law "impractical and urged direct military-to-military communication between Lebanese and Israeli forces for deconfliction," the U.S. official added.This comes a day after the White House criticized a legal complaint that was filed in Lebanon against the country's ambassador to Washington over her reported outreach to her Israeli counterpart.
5:10 PM / October 15, 2026
White House prepares plans to use weapon dubbed "mother of all bombs" on Iran, sources say
The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment."A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics.CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran.Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit.Read more here.
4:54 PM / October 15, 2026
Ousted general warned of years-long missile defense shortage before Iran war
In late December, two months before the U.S. war with Iran began, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned that his service was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last another five years, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted George in April, as the Iran war was underway.George's risk analysis appeared in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan, a defense secretary-approved annual order determining where troops and weapons will be allocated across the globe, according to the U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. He warned that the stockpile of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and Patriot missiles would continue to be strategically low until 2030. His assessment was written for the Defense Department's plan for fiscal year 2027 and before the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-led war with Iran, now in its seventh month. U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly said his assessment stemmed from the transfer of Patriots to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022, the expenditure of munitions to defend Israel, and the reduced capacity of the defense industrial base.Read more here.
2:26 PM / October 15, 2026
Asian Tour golf postpones Saudi Arabia finale
The Saudi International, the final event of the Asian Tour golf season, was postponed on Thursday following several deadly attacks on the kingdom by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.The tournament was originally scheduled to take place from Nov. 18 to 21 in Riyadh and no alternative date has been announced."The Asian Tour remains in direct contact with its players and members regarding the schedule and next steps," read a joint statement from Saudi Golf and the Asian Tour, saying the competition was postponed due to "logistical challenges."The tournament, which was part of the European Tour from 2019 to 2021, is backed by Saudi Arabia's Private Investment Fund.The postponement follows that of the Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition, which was pushed back from next week until December on Wednesday.Earlier this week, three Saudi Pro League football matches, including one involving Cristiano Ronaldo's Al Nassr, were also postponed.
1:47 PM / October 15, 2026
Lebanese president asks Rubio to press Israel to stop "assaults" in southern Lebanon
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun asked U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to press Israel on its assaults on southern Lebanon and stand by the trilateral agreement signed in June.The president's office said on X it received a call from Rubio "during which they discussed the general situation in Lebanon and the region in light of recent developments."Aoun said he requested Israel stop bulldozing operations, enable farmers to use their fields and stop targeting them, according to the Lebanese president's office. Israel patrols a so-called "security zone" in southern Lebanon to prevent attacks by the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group. As part of the trilateral agreement, Israel was supposed to progressively give control over to official Lebanese army forces. However, Israel has said they will only do so when Hezbollah completely disarms, which the group said it will not do. Aoun told Rubio that Lebanese forces have been "fully carrying out their duties in implementing decisions related to preventing armed displays" in a nod to them carrying out their part of the trilateral agreement.The State Department has not yet released a readout of the call from its side.

Saudi-led coalition says Houthis attacked Riyadh airport 20 times in October
The Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday that the Iran-backed Houthis had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times in October, as the Yemeni group escalated its strikes on the kingdom's transport hubs and oil facilities.During a presentation in Riyadh covering the strikes, coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said, "The Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure."

Saudi Arabia says Iran continues to arm, train and support Houthis
A Saudi foreign ministry official on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis in their ongoing fight with the kingdom, adding Tehran continues to arm and train the group."Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of U.N. security council resolutions," Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry, said during a virtual briefing with reporters, according to the AFP news agency."We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added later.Saudi Arabia said Thursday it had intercepted a ballistic missile in the Medina area, home to one of the holiest cities in Islam.
